# Why I'm handing over the keys to my agents

*I want to take part without living inside the feed. I'm working out how as I go.*

<!-- Revision 7, 2026-10-15. Edited down from Codex rev 6 (Sept 14, 1,137 words) to about 800 words. Same opener, same claims, no new beliefs.
     One place needs you: the [CONFIRM] line (keep, soften, or cut it). Delete this comment before publishing. -->

I want to share what I'm working on. I want to talk to people who care about the same problems. But I find the feeds overwhelming. I go in meaning to take part, get pulled away from what brought me there, and end up pulling back.

The work keeps happening. I just don't bring much of it into those conversations.

That's why I'm building Agents for Introverts. It's also why this post is late.

## The draft with a blank in it

The first version of this essay was called "Why I've *handed over* the keys to my agents." Halfway through there was a note to myself: *add the first real handoff here.* I couldn't publish until I had handed something over. I couldn't hand anything over until the tools were built. So I kept building the tools.

There's a desktop app called Quiet Desk taking shape around this practice, and I've spent weeks refining it. Meanwhile, the projects I actually wanted to talk about kept moving. [CONFIRM: Across my projects, that's well over a thousand commits since mid-September, and I posted about none of them.]

So the title changed by one word. I'm *handing over* the keys. This is the start, not a report on something finished.

## Start with the work, then talk about it

I spend my day building things, working through decisions, trying things that fail, and figuring out what to change. By the time I sit down to write, I've moved on to the next problem.

So the practice starts with the work. I use Codex's Computer History to help my agents recover context from what I did. Then we have a retrospective conversation. The agent brings a few things worth talking about. I explain why a decision mattered, what was frustrating, or what it got wrong. The history gives us somewhere specific to start. I add the reasoning and the point of view.

This essay came out of that kind of conversation. I explained why I wanted to share more, corrected the framing, and pushed back when the draft got too polished.

## One piece, many ways in

Out of those conversations, we build a piece: writing, screenshots, recordings, diagrams, sometimes an interactive example, all around one idea. A screenshot shows the interface as it was. A recording shows a sequence that's hard to describe. An illustration can explain how something works, as long as readers can tell an illustration from a record of something that happened.

Then the agent shapes versions of that piece for different places. On Substack there's room for the whole story. On LinkedIn, a decision and what it means for someone else's work might carry it. On X, one example in a short sequence. On Threads, a personal observation that invites other people's.

You're reading the Substack version. The same idea is going out on LinkedIn, X and Threads today, each told a little differently. I want those choices to be visible, keep what I mean, and point back to the fuller piece.

## Help the work find its people

A few years ago, I built Woon, an agent that lived inside iMessage. I knew how to make the product. I didn't know how to find the people who might understand it, or how to explain it in a way they could pass on to somebody else. So, more or less, I waited.

Maybe Woon was too early. Maybe it would have failed anyway. I still don't know. But I would have liked to hear from the people who could have challenged it, shaped it, or used it.

That's where I want agents to do more of the work now: finding existing conversations where something from my work could be useful, and producing a steady trickle of contributions without starting from "what should I post today?" every time.

Right now, I review every word and publish by hand. As the agents take on more, I'll show what they did, what I corrected, and why I was comfortable handing over the next part.

## Bring the conversation back

When someone asks a question, pushes back on an idea, or tells me about related work, I want to know. That's the conversation I wanted in the first place. I want the agent to bring it back with enough context that I can join in.

Those exchanges feed the next retrospective. A question might show where we explained something badly. Someone else's experience might change how I think about a decision.

Some of what I post will be about Agents for Introverts as it gets built. Most of it will be about the projects themselves: keeping an AI conversation alive across disconnects on Cloudflare, authorizing hosted MCP connectors, helping people move what their agent knows to the next one. Those will carry a short "Made with Agents for Introverts" note.

If this sounds familiar, tell me about something you built that never found its people. I'd like to hear what you tried and what you wish you'd had help with.

Tony

*Made with Agents for Introverts. My agent helped shape this version. The experience and point of view are mine.*
